arc: Stage 0 (texts 1-20), November 2026: Olga Ivanova, a nurse in Tallinn, decides to apply for Estonian citizenship. Her Estonian is already B2, so she needs only the exam on the Constitution and the Citizenship Act. Lisa gives her a copy of the Constitution, and the family reads it in the evenings: Lisa helps, Sergei asks practical questions, Nikolai remembers the past, the neighbours Mari and Jaan explain the law and the Riigikogu. Olga registers for the exam.

Stage 1 (texts 21-90), winter 2026/27: rights and freedoms in everyday life. Olga at the hospital, Lisa at school, Sergei at work, Nikolai at home; rights of everyone and rights of citizens only. A young couple from Kharkiv, Maksim and Katja Saar, in Tallinn since 2019, moves into the building. In a box of family papers Maksim finds the Estonian passport of his grandfather Johannes Saar of Tartu, who was an Estonian citizen before 1940.

Stage 2 (texts 91-130): citizenship. Olga passes the exam in December and applies at the PPA before the new year; the oath, the waiting, the Government's order. Nikolai starts his own application at 68. Maksim proves his citizenship by birth and gets his first Estonian passport; Katja starts the long road on a residence permit. Side stories: restoration for someone who lost citizenship as a minor, and loss of citizenship.

Stage 3 (texts 131-200): institutions. Jaan's work in the Riigikogu, the President, the Government and the courts, seen through the family's questions. Olga receives her citizenship certificate and her passport.
Stage 4 (texts 201-230): review by area. The family helps Katja prepare for her future exam and quizzes each other in the exam format.

slots.idea: A Tuesday evening in the family's flat in Lasnamäe. Olga tells Lisa that she wants an Estonian passport (Eesti pass); the word kodanik comes later, in text 9. Lisa takes a small blue book from her school bag: Eesti Vabariigi põhiseadus. They read § 1 together: Estonia is an independent and sovereign democratic republic, and the supreme power belongs to the people. Olga repeats the words while she cooks.

Sergei drives a lorry and knows every road. With Olga he looks at the map of Estonia on the kitchen wall: the land, the sea, the islands, Narva and Saaremaa. § 2: the land, waters and airspace are one indivisible whole; Estonia is a unitary state.

On the stairs Olga meets the neighbour Mari, a lawyer at the Chancellor of Justice's office. Mari explains § 3: the state uses its power only on the basis of the Constitution and laws, and only published laws must be followed. She shows Riigi Teataja on her phone.

Dinner at Mari and Jaan's. Jaan, a member of the Riigikogu, explains § 4 with four chairs at the table: the Riigikogu, the President, the Government and the courts. State power is separated and balanced, so no chair rules the others.

Olga writes the first page of a new notebook: republic, the power of the people, the territory, laws, the four institutions. Lisa asks her questions like an examiner, and Olga answers from the notebook.

Saturday in the forest near Tallinn with Olga's father Nikolai. He talks about the trees, the bog and the sea. § 5: the natural wealth and resources of Estonia are national riches that must be used economically.

At the hospital Olga speaks Estonian with an old patient from Tartu (side character in cast, voice albert). § 6: the official language of Estonia is Estonian. The patient praises her Estonian, and Olga says it was hard work.

Lisa paints the blue-black-white flag for a school project. On Sunday the family walks up to Toompea and sees the flag on the Tall Hermann tower. § 7: the national colours of Estonia are blue, black and white.

Mari explains § 56: the people exercise the supreme power through the citizens who have the right to vote, by electing the Riigikogu and in a referendum. Sergei asks why he cannot vote in Riigikogu elections; Mari answers that only citizens do.
The family looks at the photos of the last weeks: the forest, the hospital, the flag on Toompea, the talk about elections. Each photo brings back one §.

Lisa is 16 and asks Jaan when she can vote for the Riigikogu. § 57: Estonian citizens who are 18 vote in Riigikogu elections and referendums. Jaan adds that in local elections citizens of Estonia and of other EU states vote from 16; Lisa was 15 at the last local elections.

Side story. At a petrol station Sergei talks with a colleague (side character in cast, voice albert) whose cousin is in prison. § 58: the law may restrict the voting of citizens whom a court has convicted and who are serving a prison sentence.

Sergei, who has a grey passport, goes to the family doctor. Olga explains that the rights in the Constitution are for everyone in Estonia, also foreigners and stateless people (§ 9), and that everyone is equal before the law (§ 12).

Jaan walks with Olga and Lisa through the old town: the Riigikogu at Toompea castle has the legislative power (§ 59), the President is the head of state (§ 77), the Government in Stenbock House has the executive power (§ 86).
Olga makes flashcards about voting and the institutions, and Lisa tests her on the bus to school.

Lisa tells how she became an Estonian citizen in 2016 as a child of stateless parents: not by birth but by naturalisation. Olga writes four words from § 2 of the Citizenship Act: omandamine, saamine, taastamine, kaotamine. § 8(1) of the Constitution: a child with an Estonian citizen parent has the right to citizenship by birth.
Side story. Lisa's class visits a courtroom in Tallinn; a judge (side character in cast, voice albert) talks to the pupils. § 146: only the courts administer justice, and the courts are independent.

Olga reads the conditions for citizenship in § 6 of the Citizenship Act and ticks them off at the kitchen table: age, years of living in Estonia, Estonian, income, loyalty, the oath. Only one thing is missing: the exam on the Constitution and the Citizenship Act. Lisa helps her register for it in EIS.

Nikolai and Olga talk about loyalty. § 54: a citizen must be loyal to the constitutional order and defend the independence of Estonia. § 55: foreigners and stateless people in Estonia must observe the constitutional order. Olga reads the words of the oath of loyalty.
A quiz evening at home before the next big part, rights and freedoms. Everyone asks Olga one question about texts 16-19, and Nikolai asks the hardest one.

Late November 2026. Maksim and Katja Saar from Kharkiv, in Tallinn since 2019, move into the empty flat on the Ivanovs' floor; Sergei and Lisa help carry boxes. Katja, a Ukrainian citizen on a residence permit, asks whether a foreigner in Estonia has the same rights. Lisa reads § 9: the rights of chapter II apply equally to Estonian citizens and to foreigners and stateless people in Estonia, and (2) to legal persons as far as their nature allows; Maksim's small IT company is a legal person (juriidiline isik). Return § 12: everyone is equal before the law.

slots.idea: Nikolai invites Katja for tea and shows her his old chess set. Katja asks whether a right that the Constitution does not list exists at all. Nikolai reads § 10: the rights listed do not exclude other rights that follow from the spirit of the Constitution or are in accordance with it and with human dignity (inimväärikus) and the principles of a democratic and social state based on the rule of law. Return § 59: legislative power belongs to the Riigikogu.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Flu season at Olga's hospital: visits to the ward are limited (piirang) and a patient's son is angry. At home Mari explains § 11: rights and freedoms may be restricted only in accordance with the Constitution; restrictions must be necessary in a democratic society and must not distort (moonutama) the nature of the rights. Return § 77 as § 77 states it.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Side story in Tartu. A landlord refuses to rent a flat to Leila, a student, because of her religion; her friend Aino, a law student, reads § 12 with her: everyone is equal before the law; no one may be discriminated against on the basis of nationality, race, colour, sex, language, origin, religion, political or other opinion, property or social status, or other circumstances; inciting national, racial, religious or political hatred, violence or discrimination is prohibited and punishable. A hateful comment under Leila's post is the second scene. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md. Return § 86: the Government exercises executive power.

slots.idea: The building's house meeting in the stairwell: the new neighbours Maksim and Katja introduce themselves, and the talk returns to § 9-12: equal rights of citizens and foreigners, rights not listed, how a right may be limited, equality before the law.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Maksim unpacks a box of family papers from Kharkiv and finds the pre-war Estonian passport of his grandfather Johannes Saar of Tartu. Lisa reads § 13: everyone has the right to the protection of the state and the law; the Estonian state protects its citizens abroad too; the law protects everyone against the arbitrariness (omavoli) of state power. Maksim wonders whether he has been a citizen all along. Return § 8(1): a child with an Estonian citizen parent has the right to Estonian citizenship by birth. Nobody is sure yet; Mari will help next time.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Maksim shows Mari his grandfather's passport. Mari reads § 14: guaranteeing rights and freedoms is the duty of the legislative, executive and judicial powers and of local governments (omavalitsus). Then KodS § 2 (return): citizenship is acquired by birth, received by naturalisation, restored, or lost; Maksim's case would be acquisition by birth, so he takes no exam. Mari tells him he will need a National Archives (Rahvusarhiiv) certificate and the birth certificates; no promise of a result yet.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Sergei, a driver, gets a city decision he thinks is wrong (a parking fine from the city of Tallinn on his work van). Mari reads § 15: everyone whose rights and freedoms are violated has the right to go to court; in a case, a person may ask the court to declare unconstitutional any law, other legal act or measure that is relevant to the case. Return § 146: only courts administer justice, and they are independent. Olga worries about money; Sergei decides to complain first and go to court if needed.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Side story in Pärnu in early December. A paramedic, Svetlana, and her partner save a fisherman who fell through the ice; nobody asks who he is or what colour his skin is (nahavärvus). § 16: everyone has the right to life, protected by law, and no one may be arbitrarily deprived of life. Return KodS § 6: Svetlana is stateless and ticks off the conditions of naturalisation, like Olga. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.

slots.idea: The Saars' housewarming in early December. Each guest brings a small gift and a question about § 13-16: protection of the state and law, who guarantees rights, going to court, the right to life. Sergei tells how his fine ended; Maksim says he has written to the National Archives. Olga's exam is close.
